parts.title: Campus Conversation: Reporting a Problem in the Dorm
script: Narrator
Listen to a conversation between a student and a housing office employee.
Student
Hi. I live in Maple Hall, room 214. My heater has not worked for three days.
Staff
I'm sorry to hear that. Did you fill out a repair form online?
Student
No, I didn't know about the form. I only told my roommate.
Staff
Okay. You can fill it out on the housing website. It takes about five minutes.
Student
Can't I just tell you now? It's very cold at night.
Staff
I can write down the problem, but the repair team only accepts online forms. I will help you do it on this computer.
Student
Thank you. How long will the repair take?
Staff
Usually one or two days. A worker will call you before he comes to your room.
Student
Good. In the meantime, can I get an extra blanket?
Staff
Yes, we have extra blankets here. I will bring one to you this afternoon.
Student
That's very kind. Thank you for your help.
Narrator

parts.title: Earth Science Lecture: How Glaciers Move
script: Narrator
Listen to part of a lecture in an earth science class.
Professor
Today we will talk about glaciers. A glacier is a very large body of ice that lies on land. Many people think glaciers do not move, but in fact they move all the time.
Professor

Glaciers form in cold places where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, the snow builds up. The snow at the bottom is pressed by the weight of the snow above it, and it slowly turns into ice.
Professor
Once the ice becomes thick enough, it starts to move because of gravity. The ice flows downhill, a little like very slow honey. Most glaciers move only a few centimeters to a few meters each day.
Professor
There is a second reason glaciers move. At the bottom, a thin layer of water forms where the ice touches the ground. This water works like oil, so the glacier can slide more easily over the rock.
Professor

As a glacier moves, it changes the land. It picks up rocks and carries them for many kilometers. It also cuts deep valleys in the mountains. The wide U-shaped valleys in some countries were made by glaciers long ago.
Professor

Interestingly, the ice in a glacier can be more than ten thousand years old. Scientists drill into it and study tiny bubbles of air inside. These bubbles tell us what Earth's air was like in the past.
Professor
To review: first, glaciers form from snow that turns into ice; second, they move because of gravity and water under the ice; and third, they shape the land around them.
Narrator
Now get ready to answer the questions.
Narrator
Listen again to part of the lecture. Then answer the question.
Professor
Interestingly, the ice in a glacier can be more than ten thousand years old. Scientists drill into it and study tiny bubbles of air inside.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
questions.exp: The professor explains how glaciers form, move and shape land.

o: Snow builds up and turns into ice
Wind carries ice from the sky
questions.exp: Snow is pressed and slowly turns into ice.

questions.q: How fast do most glaciers move?
o: A few centimeters to a few meters each day
questions.exp: Most move a few centimeters to a few meters a day.

questions.q: What helps a glacier slide over the rock?
questions.exp: Water at the bottom works like oil.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention bubbles of air in the ice?
o: To show that ice is dangerous
To explain how scientists learn about the past
questions.exp: The bubbles show what Earth's air was like long ago.

questions.q: How does the professor organize the end of the lecture?
questions.exp: He says 'To review: first, second, third.'
